screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore Snowflake's Time Travel and the complementary Fail-safe service. You'll learn what Time Travel does, how to query past table states using AT and BEFORE clauses, and how to restore dropped objects with UNDROP. We'll also clarify retention settings — who can configure them, what the default durations are, and how longer retention affects storage cost. Finally, we'll contrast Time Travel with Fail-safe so you understand when you can self-serve a recovery and when Snowflake's internal disaster recovery must be involved. A concrete example will guide you: creating a small customer table, making an update and a delete, then querying the table as it existed before the change and recovering it after a drop. A common pitfall is reusing a dropped object's name immediately; that changes what UNDROP can do. By the end, you'll know how to use Time Travel for audits, quick restores, and cloning historical snapshots, and when Fail-safe is the only remaining option handled by Snowflake. Consider a recent accidental delete: with Time Travel you can usually recover right away; with Fail-safe you must contact Snowflake support and it is reserved for disaster scenarios.

screens.title: What is Time Travel?
screens.narratorSegment: Time Travel is Snowflake's built-in mechanism for accessing historical table states and recovering deleted or changed data. Technically, Snowflake retains prior micro-partitions instead of overwriting data when you run operations like UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE. Those retained micro-partitions form a record of the table's history that Snowflake can reconstruct for a period defined by the data retention setting. Practically, Time Travel feels like an undo mechanism: you can query what a table looked like at a specific timestamp or before a particular S Q L statement, and you can restore dropped objects if they remain in the Time Travel window. A typical use case is accidental data deletion: instead of restoring from an external backup, you query the table's previous state and reinsert missing rows or use UNDROP to bring back a table. A common misconception is that Time Travel is an infinite archive — it is not; retention is finite and configurable up to 90 days for standard tables, and zero for transient or temporary tables. Keep in mind that Time Travel is user-accessible and intended for operational recovery and auditing; it is distinct from Fail-safe, which is Snowflake-managed and used for disaster recovery after Time Travel expires. Reflect: when was the last time you wished for an undo for a database change?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Time Travel preserves historical micro-partitions so users can query or restore past table states for a configurable period.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › What is Time Travel?
Time Travel explained
Snowflake stores prior micro-partitions so you can query or recover historical data.
Formal definition
When data is changed, Snowflake keeps previous micro-partitions instead of overwriting them. These retained versions allow reconstruction of past table states for the retention window.
Why it matters
  • Quick recovery from accidental deletes or truncates.
  • Historical analysis and auditing without maintaining separate backups.
  • Creating clones from past snapshots for testing or debugging.
Key Takeaway

Time Travel is an operational history layer that supports self-service recovery and auditing within a configurable retention window.

Analogy
Think of Time Travel as a versioned snapshot system built into the storage layer. Each change creates a new version while old versions remain readable for the retention period.
Common misconception
It is not an indefinite archive: retention expires and then Fail-safe may apply. Also, transient tables do not retain history by default.
Concrete example
You update a customer's name, earlier micro-partitions contain the prior value. Querying with an AT timestamp returns that prior name for the retention window.

screens.title: How Snowflake preserves historical data
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake preserves history by keeping previous micro-partitions when data is changed, so new writes do not immediately overwrite earlier versions. The lifecycle begins when you run an operation that modifies data — for example, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE. Snowflake writes new micro-partitions for the changed data while retaining the old micro-partitions as historical versions. These retained partitions are discoverable and reconstructible for the duration of the table's Time Travel retention period. The retention period can be set at multiple levels — account, database, schema, or table — and Snowflake resolves the effective retention by looking at the most specific setting available. After the Time Travel window elapses, data enters Fail-safe for an additional seven days, during which only Snowflake can perform recovery for disaster scenarios. Important operational notes: transient and temporary tables default to zero days and therefore do not provide Time Travel access; increasing retention up to 90 days increases storage costs; and retention does not change the semantics of your queries, it only extends the readable history. Consider a two-step scenario: you delete rows, then two hours later query the table at a timestamp before the delete to confirm the old rows; Time Travel makes this straightforward.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Preservation process
How changes become historical versions
Step-by-step
  1. Execute a data change (UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE).
  2. Snowflake writes new micro-partitions for the modified data.
  3. Old micro-partitions are retained as historical versions.
  4. History is readable via AT or BEFORE for the retention window.
  5. After Time Travel ends, Fail-safe applies for 7 days for internal recovery.
Note: Transient/temporary tables default to zero retention and do not keep history.
Visual checklist
Retention levels: account, database, schema, table
Default retention: 1 day for standard tables
Max configurable: 90 days
Fail-safe: Snowflake-managed 7 days after Time Travel
Key Takeaway

Snowflake retains old micro-partitions to reconstruct history; configure retention carefully to balance cost and recoverability.

screens.title: Querying historical data with AT
screens.narratorSegment: The AT clause lets you read a table as it existed at a specific point in time. You can specify relative time with an OFFSET — for example, an offset of negative 3600 seconds reads data an hour ago — or an explicit TIMESTAMP value to target an exact instant. This is particularly practical when you recorded the current timestamp before making changes and want to compare before and after. A common workflow: note CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, perform your update or delete, then use AT with the recorded timestamp to extract the rows that were present earlier. Remember to choose a timestamp within the table's retention window or you won't find the earlier state. One misconception is thinking AT restores the table — it only reads historical rows. To persist the old state you either INSERT the selected rows back into the live table or use UNDROP when the object itself was dropped. In the example code panel you will see S Q L snippets that demonstrate AT with OFFSET and TIMESTAMP forms. Practice selecting historical rows, verifying results, and reinserting if you need to make the recovered state current. Always validate your selected rows before performing any write back.

keyIdea.title: AT clause
keyIdea.text: AT returns table contents as of a timestamp or offset; use it to inspect or extract historical rows within retention.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › AT clause
Query historical states with AT
Two common forms: OFFSET for relative time, TIMESTAMP for absolute time.
Examples
-- Querying data as it was 1 hour ago
SELECT * FROM my_table AT (OFFSET => -3600);

-- Querying data as it was at a specific timestamp
SELECT * FROM my_table AT (TIMESTAMP => '2023-10-25 12:00:00'::TIMESTAMP_LTZ);
Use your recorded timestamp to target exact moments. Make sure the timestamp is within retention.
Practical workflow
  1. Note CURRENT_TIMESTAMP before making changes.
  2. Perform updates or deletes.
  3. Use AT with your saved timestamp or an OFFSET to read the previous state.
  4. Validate results; INSERT rows back if you need to restore them permanently.
Key Takeaway

AT reads past states. Use it to extract and reinsert rows or to compare prior values for debugging and audits.

screens.title: Querying with BEFORE and Query ID
screens.narratorSegment: The BEFORE clause is used when you want the state of a table immediately before a particular S Q L statement executed in Snowflake. This is helpful when a single bad statement — for instance, a DELETE — removed rows and you can find the statement's unique Query ID in query history. The workflow is: locate the offending Query ID using INFORMATION_SCHEMA. QUERY_HISTORY or your query logs, then run a SELECT using BEFORE with the statement identifier. This returns the table state as it existed just before that statement ran. An important nuance: you must identify the correct Query ID for the relevant statement; similar statements may have different IDs. Also, BEFORE returns a read-only view of that prior state — to restore rows you would extract them and reinsert, or if the whole table was dropped, use UNDROP. A common misconception is that BEFORE can be used without retention — it cannot; the referenced state must still exist within Time Travel retention. Using BEFORE is particularly useful for pinpointing recovery to just before the exact change, rather than guessing a timestamp offset.

keyIdea.title: BEFORE clause
keyIdea.text: BEFORE with a statement Query ID returns the table state immediately before that statement ran; it requires locating the correct Query ID and an available retention window.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › BEFORE & Query ID
Target the moment before a statement
Find the Query ID
Search your query history for the DELETE or UPDATE statement and note its QUERY_ID.
-- Example: find the DELETE statement's Query ID
-- SELECT QUERY_ID, QUERY_TEXT FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY()) WHERE QUERY_TEXT LIKE '%DELETE FROM my_table%';

-- Then use BEFORE with that Query ID
SELECT * FROM my_table BEFORE (STATEMENT => 'abcdef12-3456-7890-abcd-ef1234567890');
BEFORE returns the exact table state just before the referenced statement executed.
Practical hints
  • Confirm the statement's timing and ensure it's within retention.
  • Validate the selected rows before re-inserting or replacing live data.
  • If the table was dropped, use UNDROP rather than BEFORE to restore the object.
Common Mistake

Using the wrong Query ID or a Query ID outside retention will return no useful historical state.

screens.title: Restoring dropped objects with UNDROP
screens.narratorSegment: UNDROP restores dropped tables, schemas, and databases if they remain within the Time Travel retention window. When you execute DROP TABLE, Snowflake marks the object as soft-deleted and retains its historical micro-partitions for the retention period. Running UNDROP TABLE brings the object back with its last state before the drop. If you drop a schema or database, UNDROP works similarly. A critical safety note: if you DROP a table and then create a new object with the exact same name, the original cannot be UNDROPped directly because the name is taken. The recommended workaround is to UNDROP the original with a new name, or drop the newly created object first and then UNDROP. Another operational detail: UNDROP restores the object in its last state; if intermediate changes occurred, you may still need AT or BEFORE to inspect earlier versions. A common misconception is thinking UNDROP covers truncation — it does not. UNDROP is for dropped objects; use AT to recover rows deleted by TRUNCATE or DELETE. In practice, perform UNDROP promptly and verify object contents before resuming dependent processes. Restoring dropped objects with UNDROP means undrop recovers soft-deleted objects within time travel; do not reuse the original name before undrop or you will block the straightforward restore.. In practical terms, undrop workflow and the safety note about name reuse. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › UNDROP workflow
Recover a dropped table
Typical commands
-- Drop and recover a table
DROP TABLE important_data;

-- Recover the table
UNDROP TABLE important_data;

-- If name is reused, UNDROP with a new name:
-- UNDROP TABLE important_data RENAME TO important_data_old;
UNDROP restores the object as it existed at drop time; confirm schema and rows after recovery.
Safety and pitfalls
  • Do not recreate the same object name if you intend to UNDROP the original.
  • If you must reuse the name, UNDROP the original under a different name and migrate data.
  • UNDROP only works within Time Travel retention; after that Fail-safe may apply and is not user-accessible.
Key Takeaway

Use UNDROP for soft-deleted objects and avoid name collisions to keep recovery simple.

screens.title: Time Travel vs Fail-safe
screens.narratorSegment: Time Travel and Fail-safe are complementary but different. Time Travel is user-facing and configurable: you can query historical data and restore objects yourself for a retention period you set, up to 90 days for standard tables. It is intended for operational recovery, auditing, and cloning historical snapshots. Fail-safe is an internal recovery service that activates after Time Travel expires and lasts seven days; it is non-configurable and is for Snowflake's internal use in catastrophic or disaster recovery scenarios. Users cannot query or access data in Fail-safe, nor can they directly recover objects from it. A common confusion is to treat Fail-safe as a backup you can call on at will — it is not. If your retention policy is too short and an incident falls outside Time Travel, you may need to work with Snowflake for Fail-safe recovery, which is not the same as a user-driven restore. The governance implication is clear: set Time Travel retention according to your recovery objectives and compliance needs instead of relying on Fail-safe as a safety net. Think of Time Travel as your daily undo and Fail-safe as a last-resort internal safeguard.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Time Travel vs Fail-safe
Side-by-side comparison
Time Travel
  • User-accessible and configurable (0–90 days).
  • Supports AT and BEFORE queries, UNDROP, and cloning from history.
  • Used for audits, ad-hoc recovery, and development snapshots.
Fail-safe
  • Internal, non-configurable 7-day period after Time Travel.
  • Accessible only to Snowflake for disaster recovery.
  • Not queryable or directly usable for user restores.
Governance recommendation
Set Time Travel retention to meet your recovery time objective and compliance needs instead of relying on Fail-safe. Longer retention increases storage cost.

screens.title: Data retention settings and implications
screens.narratorSegment: Retention determines how long historical micro-partitions remain available for Time Travel. You can configure retention at several levels: account, database, schema, and table. Snowflake evaluates the most specific setting to decide the effective retention for an object. By default, standard tables have a one-day retention; transient and temporary tables default to zero days and therefore do not expose Time Travel. You can increase retention up to 90 days for standard tables when business requirements demand longer recovery windows. However, retention increases mean more historical micro-partitions are retained and that increases storage consumption and cost. When designing a policy, weigh the business value of recoverability and auditing against the ongoing storage expense. For example, a financial ledger might justify extended retention for compliance, while short-lived staging tables could use minimal or zero retention. Also, remember that after Time Travel ends the system enters Fail-safe for seven days, reserved for Snowflake to use during catastrophic recovery. A misconception to avoid: increasing retention does not change query semantics, but it does enlarge the scope of recoverable history and storage usage. screens.title: Practical walkthrough: recover a dropped table
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a recovery scenario from the chapter using a sample customer table. First, create the table and insert two rows. Record the current timestamp so you can reference it later. Next, perform an update and a delete: change one customer's name and remove the other row. Query the table to confirm the current state. Practice these steps in a safe workspace and always validate the recovered data before trusting it in production.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Practical walkthrough
Recovering a sample table
Steps
1. Create table and insert rows. Record CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
2. UPDATE and DELETE to change and remove rows; verify current state.
3. Use AT with your saved timestamp or OFFSET to read the old state and extract needed rows.
4. If table was dropped, run UNDROP TABLE to restore within retention, then validate content.
Starter SQL (visual only)
CREATE TABLE customer_records (
  customer_id INT,
  customer_name VARCHAR(100),
  registration_date DATE
);

INSERT INTO customer_records VALUES
(1, 'Alice', '2023-01-15'),
(2, 'Bob', '2023-02-20');

-- Later
UPDATE customer_records SET customer_name = 'Alicia' WHERE customer_id = 1;
DELETE FROM customer_records WHERE customer_id = 2;

-- Query historical state
SELECT * FROM customer_records AT (OFFSET => -120);

-- If dropped
DROP TABLE customer_records;
UNDROP TABLE customer_records;

screens.title: Common mistakes and governance checklist
screens.narratorSegment: There are several common mistakes teams make when relying on Time Travel. First, not recording a timestamp before changes makes it harder to target the exact historical state; always note CURRENT_TIMESTAMP when preparing risky changes. Second, reusing a dropped object's name immediately can block a straightforward UNDROP; plan name reuse carefully or UNDROP under a different name. Third, assuming Fail-safe is user-accessible is incorrect — treat Fail-safe as Snowflake's internal last-resort mechanism and plan retention accordingly. From a governance perspective, map data criticality to retention: high-value or regulated tables may need extended retention, while staging or ephemeral tables should use minimal retention. Include cost-awareness in the policy: longer retention increases storage costs. Operationally, add verification steps after recovery: validate schema, row counts, and sample values before switching consumers back to the recovered object. For audits, use Time Travel to retrieve historical rows for evidence, but document retention windows so auditors know how far back they can inspect. Finally, automate regular checks that verify retention settings remain appropriate as data and compliance needs evolve. screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential points to remember. In this lesson we explore Snowflake's Time Travel and the complementary Fail-safe service. You'll learn what Time Travel does, how to query past table states using AT and BEFORE clauses, and how to restore dropped objects with UNDROP. We'll also clarify retention settings — who can configure them, what the default durations are, and how longer retention affects storage cost. Finally, we'll contrast Time Travel with Fail-safe so you understand when you can self-serve a recovery and when Snowflake's internal disaster recovery must be involved. A concrete example will guide you: creating a small customer table, making an update and a delete, then querying the table as it existed before the change and recovering it after a drop. A common pitfall is reusing a dropped object's name immediately; that changes what UNDROP can do. By the end, you'll know how to use Time Travel for audits, quick restores, and cloning historical snapshots, and when Fail-safe is the only remaining option handled by Snowflake. Consider a recent accidental delete: with Time Travel you can usually recover right away; with Fail-safe you must contact Snowflake support and it is reserved for disaster scenarios.

These objectives map to practical skills you should acquire while studying Time Travel and Fail-safe. First, you will be able to explain Time Travel's purpose and how historical micro-partitions let Snowflake reconstruct past table states. Second, you will use AT and BEFORE clauses to query data at a specific timestamp, by offset, or immediately before a statement, enabling audits and incremental recovery. Third, you will perform recovery operations such as UNDROP to restore dropped tables, and you will understand the constraints and safety notes around name reuse. Fourth, you will differentiate Time Travel from Fail-safe: Time Travel is user-accessible and configurable, while Fail-safe is Snowflake-managed and only available after the Time Travel window. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember: a clock for Time Travel, a query badge for AT/BEFORE, an undo box for UNDROP, and a locked shield for Fail-safe. These milestones are practical — they prepare you to recover from recent mistakes, audit data changes, and select correct retention settings balancing cost and recoverability.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical governance, cost awareness, and common recovery scenarios. One objective is to understand how retention settings are applied at account, database, schema, and table levels and how the effective retention period is resolved. You'll learn default behaviors: standard tables have a one-day default, whereas transient or temporary tables default to zero days, so Time Travel is not available for them. Another objective is to practice recovery scenarios: selecting a timestamp to query an earlier state, using a query ID to select data before a specific statement, and using UNDROP to restore removed objects. You will also learn the governance implication: increasing retention up to 90 days improves recoverability but increases storage cost, so retention is both a technical and financial policy choice. Finally, you'll be able to spot a key pitfall: re-creating a dropped object with the same name immediately prevents a straightforward UNDROP of the original object. These objectives prepare you for hands-on recovery and for advising on retention policies in your organization.

Time Travel is Snowflake's built-in mechanism for accessing historical table states and recovering deleted or changed data. Technically, Snowflake retains prior micro-partitions instead of overwriting data when you run operations like UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE. Those retained micro-partitions form a record of the table's history that Snowflake can reconstruct for a period defined by the data retention setting. Practically, Time Travel feels like an undo mechanism: you can query what a table looked like at a specific timestamp or before a particular S Q L statement, and you can restore dropped objects if they remain in the Time Travel window. A typical use case is accidental data deletion: instead of restoring from an external backup, you query the table's previous state and reinsert missing rows or use UNDROP to bring back a table. A common misconception is that Time Travel is an infinite archive — it is not; retention is finite and configurable up to 90 days for standard tables, and zero for transient or temporary tables. Keep in mind that Time Travel is user-accessible and intended for operational recovery and auditing; it is distinct from Fail-safe, which is Snowflake-managed and used for disaster recovery after Time Travel expires. Reflect: when was the last time you wished for an undo for a database change?

Snowflake preserves history by keeping previous micro-partitions when data is changed, so new writes do not immediately overwrite earlier versions. The lifecycle begins when you run an operation that modifies data — for example, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE. Snowflake writes new micro-partitions for the changed data while retaining the old micro-partitions as historical versions. These retained partitions are discoverable and reconstructible for the duration of the table's Time Travel retention period. The retention period can be set at multiple levels — account, database, schema, or table — and Snowflake resolves the effective retention by looking at the most specific setting available. After the Time Travel window elapses, data enters Fail-safe for an additional seven days, during which only Snowflake can perform recovery for disaster scenarios. Important operational notes: transient and temporary tables default to zero days and therefore do not provide Time Travel access; increasing retention up to 90 days increases storage costs; and retention does not change the semantics of your queries, it only extends the readable history. Consider a two-step scenario: you delete rows, then two hours later query the table at a timestamp before the delete to confirm the old rows; Time Travel makes this straightforward.

The AT clause lets you read a table as it existed at a specific point in time. You can specify relative time with an OFFSET — for example, an offset of negative 3600 seconds reads data an hour ago — or an explicit TIMESTAMP value to target an exact instant. This is particularly practical when you recorded the current timestamp before making changes and want to compare before and after. A common workflow: note CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, perform your update or delete, then use AT with the recorded timestamp to extract the rows that were present earlier. Remember to choose a timestamp within the table's retention window or you won't find the earlier state. One misconception is thinking AT restores the table — it only reads historical rows. To persist the old state you either INSERT the selected rows back into the live table or use UNDROP when the object itself was dropped. In the example code panel you will see S Q L snippets that demonstrate AT with OFFSET and TIMESTAMP forms. Practice selecting historical rows, verifying results, and reinserting if you need to make the recovered state current. Always validate your selected rows before performing any write back.

The BEFORE clause is used when you want the state of a table immediately before a particular S Q L statement executed in Snowflake. This is helpful when a single bad statement — for instance, a DELETE — removed rows and you can find the statement's unique Query ID in query history. The workflow is: locate the offending Query ID using INFORMATION_SCHEMA. QUERY_HISTORY or your query logs, then run a SELECT using BEFORE with the statement identifier. This returns the table state as it existed just before that statement ran. An important nuance: you must identify the correct Query ID for the relevant statement; similar statements may have different IDs. Also, BEFORE returns a read-only view of that prior state — to restore rows you would extract them and reinsert, or if the whole table was dropped, use UNDROP. A common misconception is that BEFORE can be used without retention — it cannot; the referenced state must still exist within Time Travel retention. Using BEFORE is particularly useful for pinpointing recovery to just before the exact change, rather than guessing a timestamp offset.

UNDROP restores dropped tables, schemas, and databases if they remain within the Time Travel retention window. When you execute DROP TABLE, Snowflake marks the object as soft-deleted and retains its historical micro-partitions for the retention period. In practice, perform UNDROP promptly and verify object contents before resuming dependent processes. There are several common mistakes teams make when relying on Time Travel. Second, reusing a dropped object's name immediately can block a straightforward UNDROP; plan name reuse carefully or UNDROP under a different name. Third, assuming Fail-safe is user-accessible is incorrect — treat Fail-safe as Snowflake's internal last-resort mechanism and plan retention accordingly. For audits, use Time Travel to retrieve historical rows for evidence, but document retention windows so auditors know how far back they can inspect. Let's summarize the essential points to remember. First, Time Travel is a user-accessible feature that keeps historical micro-partitions so you can query and recover table states for a configurable period up to 90 days. Second, the AT and BEFORE clauses let you read a table as of an offset, timestamp, or immediately before a specific statement identified by its Query ID. Third, UNDROP restores dropped objects within the Time Travel window, but name reuse can complicate recovery. Finally, Fail-safe is Snowflake-managed, non-configurable, and begins after Time Travel expires; it is for internal disaster recovery and is not directly usable by customers. Keep retention policies aligned with recovery objectives and cost constraints, record timestamps before risky changes, and validate recovered data before switching back to production.
